The '''One Big Beautiful Bill Act''' ('''OBBBA''') or the '''Big Beautiful Bill''' (P.L. 119-21), is a [[Law of the United States|U.S. federal statute]] passed by the [[119th United States Congress]] containing tax and spending policies that form the core of President [[Donald Trump]]'s second-term agenda. The bill was signed into law by Trump on July{{nbsp}}4, 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 3, 2025 |title=Trump to sign bill on Friday at 5 p.m., White House says |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-sign-bill-friday-5-pm-white-house-says-2025-07-03/ |access-date=July 4, 2025 |work=Reuters}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Trump signing "One Big, Beautiful Bill" into law at White House - CBS Chicago |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/video/trump-signing-one-big-beautiful-bill-into-law-at-white-house/ |access-date=2025-07-04 |website=www.cbsnews.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Although the law is popularly referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, this official short title was removed from the bill during the Senate amendment process. Therefore, the law officially has no short title.<ref>{{cite web |title=Text: H.R.1 — 119th Congress (2025-2026) |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/1/text |website=Congress.gov |publisher=Library of Congress |date=July 4, 2025 |access-date=July 10, 2025
}}</ref>

The OBBBA contains hundreds of provisions. It permanently extends the individual tax rates [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act|Trump signed into law in 2017]], which were set to expire at the end of 2025. It raises the cap on the [[state and local tax deduction]] to $40,000 for taxpayers making less than $500,000, with the cap reverting to $10,000 after five years. The OBBBA includes several tax deductions for tips, overtime pay, auto loans, and creates [[Trump account]]s, allowing parents to create tax-deferred accounts for the benefit of their children, all set to expire in 2028. It includes a permanent $200 increase in the child tax credit, a 1%{{nbsp}}tax on [[remittance]]s, and a tax hike on investment income from college endowments. It phases out some clean energy tax credits that were included in the [[Biden presidency|Biden]]-era [[Inflation Reduction Act]], and promotes fossil fuels over renewable energy. It increases a tax credit for advanced semiconductor manufacturing and repeals a tax on [[Silencer (firearms)|silencers]].<ref name="Cooper and Dayen 2025">{{cite web | last1=Cooper | first1=Ryan | last2=Dayen | first2=David | title=Ten Bizarre Things Hidden in Trump's Big Beautiful Bill | website=The American Prospect | date=July 7, 2025 | url=https://prospect.org/politics/2025-07-07-ten-bizarre-things-hidden-in-trumps-big-beautiful-bill/ | access-date=July 8, 2025}}</ref>

It raises the [[United States debt ceiling|debt ceiling]] by $5{{nbsp}}trillion while making a significant 12%{{nbsp}}cut to [[Medicaid]] spending.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Parlapiano |first1=Alicia |last2=Sanger-Katz |first2=Margot |date=2025-07-03 |title=9 Questions About the Republican Megabill, Answered |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/03/upshot/republican-bill-faq.html |access-date=2025-07-06 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The OBBBA expands work requirements for [[SNAP benefits]] (formerly called "food stamps") recipients and makes states responsible for some costs relating to the food assistance program. The OBBBA includes $150{{nbsp}}billion in new defense spending and another $150{{nbsp}}billion for border enforcement and [[Deportation in the second presidency of Donald Trump|deportations]]. The law increases the funding for [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement|Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) from $10{{nbsp}}billion to more than $100{{nbsp}}billion by 2029, making it the single most funded federal law enforcement agency.

The [[Congressional Budget Office]] (CBO) estimates the law will increase the budget deficit by $2.8{{nbsp}}trillion by 2034 and cause 10.9{{nbsp}}million Americans to lose [[health insurance coverage in the United States|health insurance coverage]]. Further CBO analysis estimated the highest 10% of earners would see incomes rise by 2.7% by 2034 mainly due to tax cuts, while the lowest 10% would see incomes fall by 3.1% mainly due to cuts to programs such as Medicaid and food aid. Several think tanks, experts, and opponents criticized the bill over its [[regressive tax]] structure, described many of its policies as gimmicks, and argued the bill would create the largest upward transfer of wealth from the poor to the rich in American history, exacerbating [[wealth inequality in the United States|inequality among the American population]]. It has also drawn controversy for rolling back [[renewable energy|clean energy]] incentives and increasing funding for immigration enforcement and deportations. According to multiple polls, a majority of Americans oppose the law.

[[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] opposition to the health spending cuts included in the OBBBA contributed to the [[2025 United States federal government shutdown]].

==Background==
[[File:Donald Trump Signs One Big Beautiful Bill into Law.png|thumb|President Trump signing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law on the White House South Lawn on July 4, 2025]]

Following the [[2024 United States elections]], in which the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] retained the [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] and won the [[United States Senate|Senate]], Republicans began negotiations on passing then-president-elect [[Donald Trump]]'s domestic policies. In a meeting with Senate Republicans in December 2024, Senate majority leader [[John Thune]] outlined an approach involving initial legislation on border security, energy production, and the military while reserving tax policy.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.wsj.com/politics/senate-republicans-aim-to-tackle-border-first-taxes-later-98026ef8 |title=Senate Republicans Aim to Tackle Border First, Taxes Later |date=December 3, 2024 |last=Rubin |first=Richard |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |access-date=February 25, 2025}}</ref> Trump, in contrast, advocated for a singular bill to resolve an impending lapse in tax cuts implemented in the [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act]] in 2017. However, this strategy faced risks from defecting members.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/republicans-lean-toward-one-big-beautiful-bill-for-trump-agenda-11eb63bc |title=Republicans Lean Toward 'One Big, Beautiful Bill' for Trump Agenda |date=January 4, 2025 |last1=Rubin |first1=Richard |last2=Hughes |first2=Siobhan |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |access-date=February 25, 2025 |archive-date=March 17, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250317204733/https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/republicans-lean-toward-one-big-beautiful-bill-for-trump-agenda-11eb63bc |url-status=live}}</ref>

In January 2025, Republicans met in [[Fort Lesley J. McNair]]. At the meeting, Speaker of the House [[Mike Johnson]] stated that Trump sought "one big, beautiful bill" to enact his policies.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2025/01/04/johnson-trump-reconciliation-package-00196487 |title=Johnson tells House Republicans that Trump wants one 'big beautiful' reconciliation package |date=January 4, 2025 |last1=Diaz |first1=Danielle |last2=Hill |first2=Meredith |last3=Carney |first3=Jordain |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=February 25, 2025}}</ref> To more easily pass the bill, Republicans chose to use the [[Reconciliation (United States Congress)|budget reconciliation]] process,<ref name="CBS-news-2025-TR">{{cite news |last=Hubbard |first=Kaia |date=July 1, 2025 |title=Here's what's in Trump's "big, beautiful bill" that passed the Senate |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/whats-in-trump-big-beautiful-bill-senate-version/ |publisher=CBS News |access-date=July 3, 2025}}</ref> which allowed them to avoid the [[Filibuster in the United States Senate|60-vote Senate filibuster]], which carried importance as they hold 53 seats out of 100 in the Senate. This requires the House and the Senate to pass identical instructions before passing the actual reconciliation bill.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Davis |first1=Jeff |title=The Rule That Broke the Senate |url=https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2017/10/15/how-budget-reconciliation-broke-congress-215706/ |access-date=March 29, 2019 |work=Politico |date=October 15, 2017}}</ref>

Before being signed into law, the Senate approved the bill 51–50 on July 1, 2025, with Vice President [[JD Vance]] casting a tiebreaking vote in support. It passed the House of Representatives, 218–214, on July 3, 2025. It passed over universal [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] opposition in both houses.

Bill, and How Much It Would Cost or Save |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/06/30/upshot/senate-republican-megabill.html |access-date=July 2, 2025 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Duehren |first=Andrew |date=2025-06-29 |title=Senate Bill Would Add at Least $3.3 Trillion to Debt, Budget Office Says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/29/us/politics/senate-bill-trump-cbo-score-debt.html |access-date=2025-07-03 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and to cut approximately $4.46{{nbsp}}trillion in tax revenue.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 29, 2025 |title=Estimated Budgetary Effects of an Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute to H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Relative to CBO's January 2025 Baseline {{!}} Congressional Budget Office |url=https://www.cbo.gov/publication/61534 |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=www.cbo.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref name="nbcoverview">{{Cite web |last1=Tsirkin |first1=Julie |last2=Thorp V |first2=Frank |last3=Kapur |first3=Sahil |date=June 30, 2025 |title=Here's what's in the Senate's version of the 'big, beautiful bill' |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/trump-big-beautiful-bill-senate-tax-medicaid-cuts-rcna216024 |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=NBC News}}</ref>

=== Individual income taxes===
==== Extending 2017 tax cuts ====
The law permanently extends the individual tax rates [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act|Trump signed into law in 2017]], which were set to expire at the end of 2025.<ref name="signed_law">{{cite news |last1=Freking |first1=Kevin |last2=Mascaro |first2=Lisa |url=https://apnews.com/article/what-is-republican-trump-tax-bill-f65be44e1050431a601320197322551b |title=What's in the tax and spending bill that Trump has signed into law |work=[[AP News]] |date=July 5, 2025 |access-date=July 5, 2025}}</ref><ref name="CBS, Here's what's in Trump's ‘big, beautiful,’ July 4, 2025">{{Cite news |date=July 14, 2025 |title=Here's what's in Trump's 'big, beautiful bill' passed by Congress |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/whats-in-trump-big-beautiful-bill-senate-version/ |work=CBS }}</ref>

==== Tax deduction for qualified overtime income ====
The law creates a new tax deduction of up to $12,500 ($25,000 if married filing jointly) of qualified overtime pay, effective January 1, 2025.<ref name= wood>Wood, Christopher (July 22, 2025). "[https://tax.thomsonreuters.com/blog/retroactive-tax-law-for-tips-and-overtime-demands-immediate-action-payroll-expert-cautions/ Retroactive tax law for tips and overtime demands immediate action, payroll expert cautions]". ''Thomson Reuters''.</ref>

Qualified overtime pay is compensation that an employer is required to pay an employee under the [[Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938|Fair Labor Standards Act, Section 7]] because the employee worked more than 40 hours during the same workweek. The employee may take a tax deduction only for the extra half-time pay above their usual hourly rate they are paid for working more than 40 hours during the same workweek, not all the pay they receive for working those hours.<ref name= wood/> Overtime paid that is either paid voluntarily by an employer, is paid based on contractual agreements, or is only required by state or local laws is not eligible for the tax deduction.<ref>"[https://www.nahb.org/blog/2025/07/overtime-tips-taxes What to Know about “No Tax on Overtime” and “No Tax on Tips”]". ''National Association of Home Builders''. 2025.</ref><ref>"[https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/one-big-beautiful-bill-act-impact-on-employee-benefits One Big Beautiful Bill Act Impact on Employee Benefits]". ''Crowell & Moring LLP''. 2025.</ref> Overtime pay continues to be subject to Social Security tax and Medicare tax.<ref name= rsm>"[https://rsmus.com/insights/services/business-tax/big-beautiful-bill-compensation-and-benefits-tax.html How the OBBBA affects tax treatment of compensation and benefits]". ''RSM US LLP''. July 10, 2025.</ref>

The deduction begins to phase out for individuals whose [[modified adjusted gross income]] is more than $150,000 (or $300,000 if married filing jointly), and is eliminated at $400,000 (or $550,000 if married filing jointly).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/one-big-beautiful-bill-act-tax-deductions-for-working-americans-and-seniors |title=One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act: Tax deductions for working Americans and seniors |date=July 14, 2025 |work=Internal Revenue Service |access-date=December 12, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.shepherdfinancialpartners.com/new-phaseout-limits-for-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act/ |date=September 16, 2025 |title=New Phaseout Limits for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act |access-date=December 12, 2025}}</ref>{{efn|Modified adjusted gross income is the sum of adjusted gross income and all gross income excluded as foreign earned income, foreign housing allowance, [[Guam]]-source income, [[American Samoa]]-source income, [[Northern Mariana Islands]]-source income, or [[Puerto Rico]]-source income.}}

Individuals may take a tax deduction for the amount of qualified overtime compensation that appears on their [[Form W-2]], which employers will be required to include on it.<ref name= rsm/> Employers may use a reasonable method to approximate the amount to put on a Form W-2 for 2025, or via an alternate method.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://mrsc.org/stay-informed/mrsc-insight/november-2025/no-tax-on-overtime |title=
What Employers Should Know About the "No Tax on Overtime" Provisions |author=Julie Nicoll |work=Municipal Research and Services Center |date=November 19, 2025}}</ref> The [[Internal Revenue Service]] will release new procedures for federal tax withholding effective 2026.<ref>Barnes, Justin R.; Brecher, Jeffrey W.; Ekelman, Felice B.; Ostrower, Melissa; Peck, Amy L.; Thomas, Kellie M. (July 10, 2025). "[https://www.jacksonlewis.com/insights/federal-obbba-round-what-employers-need-know-now Federal OBBBA Round-Up: What Employers Need to Know Now]". ''Jackson Lewis''.</ref>

==== Tax deduction for qualified tip income ====
The law creates new [[No tax on tips|tax deductions for tips]] of up to $25,000 per year received by workers earning less than $150,000, with the tax deduction set to expire in 2028.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chabot |first=Hillary |date=July 1, 2025 |title=What Ending Taxes on Tips Could Mean for Workers and Tippers · Babson Thought & Action |url=https://entrepreneurship.babson.edu/no-tax-on-tips/ |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=Babson Thought & Action |language=en}}</ref>

In order to be eligible, a tip must be paid voluntarily by the payor, and the payor must determine the amount of the tip.<ref name= n2025-69>"[Notice 2025-69: Guidance for Individual Taxpayers who received Qualified Tips or Qualified Overtime Compensation in 2025 Notice 2025-69 https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-25-69.pdf]". ''Internal Revenue Service''. 2025.</ref> The payor must not be subject to a penalty if they do not pay a tip, and the tips must not be subject to any negotiation.<ref name= n2025-69/>

The tip must be given to a workers working one of 68 different job types.{{efn| According to a preliminary list released by the U.S. Department of Treasury, the occupations are bartenders, wait staff, food services in non-restaurants, dining room and cafeteria attendants and bartender helpers; chefs and cooks; food preparation workers; fast food and counter workers; dishwashers; restaurant hosts; bakers; gambling dealers; gambling change persons and booth cashiers; gambling cage workers; gambling and sports book writers and runners; dancers; musicians and singers; DJs not working in radio; entertainers and performers; digital content creators; ushers, lobby attendants, and ticket takers; locker room, coatroom, and dressing room attendants; baggage porters and bellhops; concierges; hotel, motel, and resort desk clerks; maids and housekeeping cleaners; home maintenance and repair workers; home landscaping and groundskeeping workers; home electricians; home plumbers; home heating and air conditioning mechanics and installers; home appliance installers and repairers; home cleaning service workers; locksmiths; roadside assistance workers; personal care and service workers; private event planners; private event and portrait photographers; private event videographers; event officiants; pet caretakers; tutors; nannies and babysitters; skincare specialists; massage therapist; barbers, hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists; shampooers; manicurists and pedicurists; eyebrow threading and waxing technicians; makeup artists; exercise trainers and group fitness instructors; tattoo artists and piercers; tailors; shoe and leather workers and repairers; golf caddies; self-enrichment teachers; recreational and tour pilots; tour guides and escorts; travel guides; sports and recreation instructors; parking and valet attendants; taxi and rideshare drivers and chauffeurs; shuttle drivers; goods delivery people; personal vehicle and equipment cleaners; private and charter bus drivers; water taxi operators and charter boat workers; rickshaw, pedicab, and carriage drivers; and home movers.<ref name= tiplist/>}}<ref>"[https://www.adp.com/spark/articles/2025/09/early-guidance-issued-under-hr-1-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act.aspx Early Guidance Issued under H.R. 1, The One Big Beautiful Bill Act]". ''ADP''. September 15, 2025.</ref><ref name=tiplist>"[https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/136/Tipped-Occupations-Detailed-8-27-2025.pdf Occupations That Customarily and Regularly Received Tips on or Before December 31, 2024]". ''U.S. Department of Treasury''. September 2, 2025.</ref>

Tips received while performing a service that is a felony or misdemeanor are not eligible.{{efn| The federal register gives an example of a bartender who works in a jurisdiction where a license or certification is required by law in order to work in that occupation but the bartender does not have that license or certification. The tips given to that bartender would not be eligible.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13>"[https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-07104.pdf Final Rule: Occupations that Customarily and Regularly Received Tips; Definition of Qualified Tips]". ''Federal Register''. Internal Revenue Service. U.S. Department of Treasury. April 13, 2026.</ref> }}<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/> Tips received for prostitution or pornography are not eligible.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/>

Tips received as part of a tip pool are generally eligible.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/> Tips received directly by a supervisor or manager are eligible only if they are for services they provided in a qualified occupation and not as part of a tip pool.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/>

If the customer is charged a service charge or an automatic tip amount that is not voluntary on the part of the customer, then the service charge or tip is not eligible.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/> This includes if the company requires a customer to pay a service charge or a particular tip amount on parties greater than a certain size.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/> Voluntary tips above such a minimum or mandatory charge are eligible.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/> Recommended tips are eligible if they are optional on the part of the payer.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/>

If the customer is required to select a tip amount but does not have the option to choose to not tip at all, the minimum possible tip amount is not eligible but any tips exceeding that minimum are eligible.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/>

If a customer has the right to receive additional goods or services in exchange for a voluntary tip, the tip is not eligible.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/>

The tax deduction is not allowed if the individual is married and files their federal income tax return separately from their spouse.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/>

The tax deduction is not allowed if the individual does not include their social security number on their federal income tax return or if the social security number was issued on or after the due date, including extensions, of the federal income tax return .<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/>

For a self-employed individual who receives tips in the course of their trade or business, eligible tips are tax deductible but they cannot create a net loss for the trade or business.<ref name= fed-reg-apr-13/>

==== Tax deductible for loan interest for U.S.-assembled cars ====
The law allows individuals to deduct up to $10,000 per year in auto loan interest for new cars that had their final assembly in the United States and were purchased between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2028.<ref name= which>{{Cite web |last=T aylor |first= Kelley R. |date= May 29, 2025 |title= New GOP Car Loan Tax Deduction: Which Vehicles and Buyers Qualify |url= https://www.kiplinger.com/taxes/new-gop-car-loan-tax-deduction |access-date= July 1, 2025 |work= Kiplinger |language=en}}</ref>

The vehicle must be for personal use, rather than business use.<ref>"[https://s-bcpas.com/obbba-auto-loan-interest-tax-deduction/ OBBBA Auto Loan Interest Tax Deduction]". ''SpieglerBlevins''. 2025.</ref> It must be a car, minivan, van, sport utility vehicle, pickup truck, or motorcycle with a gross vehicle weight rating of less than 14,000 pounds.<ref name= hulem>Hulem, Julie; Sakats, Mark (July 16, 2025). "[https://www.grfcpa.com/resource/auto-loan-interest-deduction/ Tax Alert: Introduction of Auto Loan Interest Deduction]". ''GRF CPAs and Advisors''.</ref> All-terrain vehicles, trailers, campers, used vehicles, and leased vehicles are not eligible.<ref name= hulem/> The vehicle's [[Monroney sticker|Automobile Information Disclosure label]] must show that the place of its final assembly was the United States.<ref name= which/> The maximum tax deduction is reduced out for individuals whose modified adjusted gross income is greater than $100,000 (or $200,000 for married couples filing jointly), and it is eliminated for individuals whose modified adjusted gross income is greater than $150,000 (or $250,000 if married filing jointly).<ref name= schwartz>"[https://www.schwartzschwartz.com/blog/2025/7/6/new-deduction-for-car-loan-interest-what-the-no-tax-on-car-loans-provision-means-for-you New Deduction for Car Loan Interest: What the 'No Tax on Car Loans' Provision Means for You]". ''Schwartz Schwartz''. July 6, 2025.</ref> A taxpayer is not required to itemize their tax deductions in order to take the tax deduction.<ref name= jarrett>Jarrett, Sandi (August 14, 2025). "[https://kaufmanrossin.com/blog/major-changes-to-deductions-under-the-obbba-what-taxpayers-need-to-know-for-2025-and-beyond/ The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) introduces significant changes to both itemized and standard deductions beginning with the 2025 tax year]". ''Kaufman Rossin Group''.</ref>

From 2025 to 2028, auto loan lenders are required to report loan details to the Internal Revenue Service if they receive at least $600 of interest on qualifying vehicle loans.<ref name= schwartz/>

==== Increased limit for tax deductions for state and local taxes ====
From January 1, 2025, to December 31, 2029, individuals may take a tax deduction for up to $40,000 of [[state and local tax deduction|state and local taxes]] ($20,000 if married filing separately), which is an increase from $10,000 previously.<ref name= ghj>Dubey, Arun; Gutierrez, Frances Ellington; Meadow, Nathaniel (July 28, 2025). "[https://www.ghjadvisors.com/ghj-insights/state-tax-considerations-one-big-beautiful-bill-act State Tax Considerations from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act]". ''Green Hasson & Janks LLC''.</ref> There is a reduction to the limit for the tax deduction for individuals whose modified adjusted gross income is over $500,000 ($250,000 for married filing separately) but it never goes below $10,000.<ref name= ghj/><ref name= adp>"[https://www.adp.com/spark/articles/2025/07/hr-1-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act-enacted-july-4-2025.aspx H.R.1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Enacted July 4, 2025]" ''[[ADP (company)|ADP]]''. July 10, 2025.</ref>

This provision has an estimated cost of $142{{nbsp}}billion. Republican representatives [[Elise Stefanik]], [[Mike Lawler]], [[Nick LaLota]], and [[Andrew Garbarino]] of New York, Representative [[Young Kim]] of California, and Representative [[Tom Kean Jr.]] of New Jersey cut this deal with House speaker Mike Johnson in exchange for their votes.{{citation needed|date=July 2025}}

==== Tax credit for seniors ====
The law permanently eliminates the [[personal exemption]], which had been temporarily eliminated by the [[Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017]]. It offers a temporary tax deduction, set to expire in 2028, of up to $6,000 for seniors. The deduction phases out for individuals with [[modified adjusted gross income]] (MAGI) exceeding $75,000 (or $150,000 for married couples).<ref name="signed_law"/> According to the [[Council of Economic Advisers|Council of Economic Advisors]], this would result in 88% of seniors being able to claim enough deductions to clear their [[Social Security (United States)|Social Security]] tax burden, up from 64% under prior law.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Demirjian |first=Karoun |date=July 1, 2025 |title=Trump Exaggerates His Agenda Bill's Impact on Social Security Taxes |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/01/us/politics/trump-bill-social-security-taxes.html |access-date=July 1, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] }}</ref> A taxpayer is not required to itemize their tax deductions in order to take the tax deduction.<ref name= jarrett/>

==== Child tax credit ====
The law increases the maximum amount of the [[Child tax credit (United States)|child tax credit]] from $2,000 to $2,200 per child, and indexes the amount of the credit to inflation and only applies to U.S citizens or qualifying noncitizens.{{efn| For the child tax credit, a qualifying noncitizen is an individual (or their spouse, if married filing jointly) who has a social security number that is valid for U.S. employment and that was assigned to them before their income tax return's due date including extensions.<ref>"[https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/individuals/child-tax-credit Child Tax Credit]". ''Internal Revenue Service''. November 18, 2025.</ref>}}<ref name="signed_law"/><ref name="part">{{cite news |last=Ockerman |first=Emma |url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/child-tax-credit-gets-small-boost-in-trumps-tax-bill-but-millions-of-families-are-left-out-215136488.html |title=Child tax credit gets small boost in Trump's tax bill, but millions of families are left out |work=[[Yahoo Finance]] |date= |access-date=July 5, 2025}}</ref> The refundable portion of the credit is also indexed to inflation, but is not increased, meaning that tax credit beneficiaries would not see a net increase in the credit, when adjusted for inflation.<ref name="part"/>

The law changes the existing nonrefundable tax credit for up to $17,280 of qualified adoption expenses.<ref>Erickson, Mitchell (July 23, 2025). ==== Charitable contributions tax deduction ====
Effective January 1, 2026, the law allows a tax deduction for charitable contributions made in cash by an individual who does not itemize their tax deductions. The deduction is limited to $1,000 (or $2,000 if married filing jointly). The deduction is not allowed for contributions to [[donor-advised fund]]s or private non-operating foundations. Carrying over excess charitable contributions to other years is not allowed if the person does not itemize their tax deductions.<ref name= key/><ref name= fid-char>"[https://www.fidelitycharitable.org/articles/obbb-tax-reform.html One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB): Impact on charitable giving]". ''Fidelity Charitable''. 2025.</ref><ref>{{USC|26|170}}(p)</ref>

Effective January 1, 2026, for individuals who itemize their tax deductions, a tax deduction is allowed only for the amount that exceeds 0.5{{nbsp}}percent of their [[adjusted gross income]].{{efn|For this purpose, adjusted gross income is calculated without reducing it by the amount of charitable contributions made.<ref name= key/>}}<ref name= key/><ref name= fid-char/>

The law makes permanent a temporary limit on cash tax deductions for charitable contributions of up to 60{{nbsp}}percent of their adjusted gross income to [[501(c)(3)]] public charities. This only applies if the individual itemizes their tax deductions.<ref name= key/><ref name= fid-char/>

Effective January 1, 2026, the tax benefit for charitable contributions made by an individual that itemizes their tax deductions is limited to 35% of the amount contributed, even if they are in a marginal tax bracket higher than 35%.<ref name= key/><ref name= fid-char/>

==== Educator tax deduction ====
Previously, educators could take a tax deduction for unreimbursed education costs of up to $300 per year (or $600 if married filing jointly) without itemizing their tax deductions. Effective January 1, 2026, eligible educators may also take an itemized tax deduction for unreimbursed education costs in excess of $300 per year (or $600 if married filing jointly). In order to qualify, the individual must work at any K–12 school for least 900 hours during the school year as a teacher, instructor, counselor, principal, aide, interscholastic sports coach, or sports administrator. The unreimbursed education costs must be directly related to the individual's work as an educator. Eligible unreimbursed education costs include books, supplies, other classroom materials, equipment, professional development courses or training that is related to the curriculum or student instruction.<ref>Bedolla, Regina (August 1, 2025). "[https://www.parksaccounting.com/post/new-rules-for-educator-expenses-under-ob3-what-teachers-coaches-need-to-know Parks Tax & Consulting PLLC]". ''Parks Tax & Consulting PLLC''.</ref>

Itemized deductions are reduced by 2/37 of the lesser of the amount of the itemized tax deductions or the taxable income that is within the 37%-rate marginal tax bracket.{{efn|For 2025, the 37%-rate tax bracket applies to taxable income exceeding $626,350 (or $751,600 if married filing jointly). As an exception, the qualified business income deduction under {{USC|26|199A}} is not subject to the limitation.<ref name= weinberger/>

==== Remittance tax ====
Effective January 1, 2026, the law establishes a 1% excise tax on certain electronic transfers of funds from the United States to a foreign country.{{efn|The House bill called for a 3.5% tax, but would have reimbursed [[U.S. citizens]]. The Senate version, which was eventually enacted, was estimated to raise up to $10{{nbsp}}billion over 10 years.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 30, 2025 |title=GOP remittance tax in megabill projected to raise a lot more money, despite lower rate |url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2025/06/30/congress/gop-remittance-tax-plan-said-to-raise-a-lot-more-money-despite-lower-rate-00433068 |publisher=Politico}}</ref>}} The tax is on the electronic transfer of funds from an individual located in any U.S. state, U.S. territory, or the District of Columbia to a recipient in a foreign country for personal, family, or household purposes.<ref name="baker">"[https://insightplus.bakermckenzie.com/bm/attachment_dw.action?attkey=3fVUZOjc8PCkIZ2VsS1SKt4W23K%2BGfSKBwyJWupCDsEFft1X0kSZ5qZ%2B0sE2nBoFYeoP%2Bk%2Bj%2BV%2BeCPYrGiPX%2BDSKqhfJWXA%3D&nav=%2FAtUMqQBRHG%2B%2BguzIBjghgqs75NKBsj1QsnZ3dnQzcnYwQ8iXAKc9LPk5GPIuhlH9KlhBKcWz04%3D&attdocparam=LZ52tJGUAw3FomsoXmOuKc6kj5vh8ob2DhV2DzLPEybYx8Zf2hYoi52ar06ccKba0QW7YYCzCdMJuRY%3D&fromContentView=1 United States: OBBBA Introduces New Excise Tax on Remittance Transfers]". ''Baker & McKenzie''. July 2025.</ref>

The excise tax is assessed on electronic transfers sent using cash, [[money order]]s, [[cashier's check]]s, prepaid card reloads, wire transfers, online bill payments, and similar methods.<ref name="mayerbrown">Goldberger, Jared B.; Beam, David L.; Bisanz, Matthew; Lopez Valek, Juan F.; Payne, Warren S.; Burrall, Julie S.; Newsom, Alexandra J. (July 28, 2025)." [https://www.mayerbrown.com/en/insights/publications/2025/07/what-the-new-remittance-transfer-excise-tax-means-for-businesses What the New Remittance Transfer Excise Tax Means for Businesses]". ''Mayer Brown''.</ref> The excise tax is assessed on the amount transferred and not on any fees that the sending institution charges the sender to complete the transfer.<ref name="mayerbrown" /> The excise tax is supposed to be paid by the sender of the remittance; the transfer provider must pay the excise tax if the sender does not.<ref name="remittance">{{cite web |last=Fontaine |first=Rebeccah |date=August 13, 2025 |title=Implications of the Remittance Tax in the GOP Reconciliation Bill |url=https://www.eisneramper.com/insights/tax/remittance-tax-implications-obbba-0725/ |publisher=EisnerAmper}}</ref> A transfer to a U.S. military base located in a foreign country are considered to be received in the United States and is not subject to the remittance tax.<ref name= Schostag>Schostag, Keith (August 28, 2025). "[https://www.americascreditunions.org/blogs/compliance/what-included-remittance-transfer-tax What is Included in the Remittance Transfer Tax?]" ''America's Credit Unions''.</ref> Additionally, transfers of $15 or less are not subject to the remittance tax.<ref name= Schostag/>

Certain transfers are exempt, such as those from financial accounts held at institutions subject to the [[Bank Secrecy Act]], such as [[bank|U.S. bank]]s, [[credit union|U.S. credit union]]s, [[investment companies|U.S. investment companies]], and certain U.S. branches of foreign banks; transfers paid with a U.S.-issued debit or credit card; and transfers of [[cryptocurrency]].<ref name="baker" /><ref name="mayerbrown" /><ref name="remittance" />

The [[Estate tax in the United States|estate]], [[gift tax|gift]], and [[generation-skipping transfer tax]] exemption will increase from $13.99{{nbsp}}million in 2025 to $15{{nbsp}}million in 2026. The exemption amounts for subsequent years will be indexed for inflation.<ref>Constantine, Sarah; Koss, Cara M.; Rosenstock, Coryn G. (July 21, 2025). ''Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP''.</ref>

====Qualified small business stock gain exclusion====
The [[Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993]] allowed noncorporate taxpayers who acquired [[Qualified Small Business Stock|qualified small business stock]] and held the stock for more than five years to exclude from [[capital gains tax in the United States|capital gain recognition]] of up to $10{{nbsp}}million or 10 times the taxpayer's basis in the stock, which ever was greater. In order for the stock to qualify, the issuing corporation's aggregate gross assets needed to be no more than $50{{nbsp}}million immediately before or after the stock issuance.<ref name= nance>Nance, Ryan (November 30, 2025). "[https://www.thetaxadviser.com/issues/2025/nov/qsbs-gets-a-makeover-what-tax-pros-need-to-know-about-sec-1202s-new-look/ QSBS gets a makeover: What tax pros need to know about Sec. 1202’s new look]". ''The Tax Adviser''. Association of International Certified Professional Accountants.</ref>

The OBBBA changed the requirement to hold the stock for at least five years. For qualified small business stock acquired after July 4, 2025, a 50% exclusion is available for stock held at least three years, a 75% exclusion is available for stock held for at least four years, and a 100% continues to be available for stock held for at least five years.<ref name= nance/>

The OBBBA also increased the exclusion's limit to $15{{nbsp}}million or 10 times the taxpayer's basis in the stock, which ever was greater. The $15-million limit will be subject to annual inflation adjustments in 2027 and thereafter.<ref name= nance/>

In addition, the OBBBA now allows the issuing corporation to have an aggregate gross asset limitation of up to $75{{nbsp}}million for stock issued after July 4, 2025. The $75-million limit will be subject to annual inflation adjustments in 2027 and thereafter.<ref name= nance/>

=== Business income taxes===
====Tax deduction for executive compensation====
[[Public company|Public companies]] are not allowed to take a tax deduction for compensation paid to certain executives that exceeds $1{{nbsp}}million per year.<ref>{{USC|26|162|a}}</ref> Effective tax years beginning after December 31, 2026, the compensation paid to the five most highly compensated executives is expanded to all members of a covered corporation's controlled group and affiliated service group. The tax deductible portion of compensation is allocated to each control group member based on the pro-rata portion of the compensation paid by that member.<ref name= covington>"[https://www.cov.com/news-and-insights/insights/2025/07/key-provisions-of-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act Key Provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act]". ''[[Covington & Burling LLP]]''. July 9, 2025.</ref>

==== Depreciation tax deduction ====
For qualified production property of a taxpayer, the law makes permanent a 100% [[Section 179 depreciation deduction]] for the [[adjusted basis]] for the property acquired after January 19, 2025.<ref name="auto7"/><ref name="Stamper 2025">{{cite web | last=Stamper | first=Dustin | title=Incentivizing Production: What the OBBBA Means for Manufacturing | website=BDO USA, P.C. | date=August 4, 2025 | url=https://www.bdo.com/insights/industries/manufacturing/incentivizing-production-what-the-obbba-means-for-manufacturing | access-date=August 16, 2025}}</ref><ref name="Grant Thornton 2025">{{cite web | title=OBBBA offers new ways to accelerate depreciation | website=Grant Thornton | date=August 4, 2025 | url=https://www.grantthornton.com/insights/alerts/tax/2025/insights/obbba-offers-new-ways-to-accelerate-depreciation | access-date=August 16, 2025}}</ref>

Businesses are allowed to take a [[section 179]] tax deduction for the cost of certain business property, software, leasehold improvements, and water utility property rather than deduct only the amount depreciated each year. Under the law, the maximum tax deduction is permanently increased from $1{{nbsp}}million to $2.5{{nbsp}}million and then phased out to $4{{nbsp}}million, all of which will be indexed for inflation in future years. These changes are effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.<ref>Berry, Ken (October 8, 2025). "[https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2025/10/08/2025-tax-law-improves-incentives-for-business-property-obbba/170328/ 2025 Tax Law Improves Incentives for Business Property (OBBBA)]". ''CPA Practice Advisor''. Firmworks, LLC.</ref>

The law also created a new depreciation allowance for nonresidential real property that is used as an essential part of an activity that includes the manufacturing, production, or refining of certain tangible products that significantly transforms the product. Types of property that do not qualify include nonresidential real property used for offices, administrative services, lodging, parking, sales activities, software development, and software engineering. The property's construction must begin between January 20, 2025, and December 31, 2028, and it must be placed in service in the U.S. or U.S. possessions on or before December 31, 2030.<ref name= key>[https://www.cov.com/en/news-and-insights/insights/2025/07/key-provisions-of-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act Key Provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act]". ''Covington & Berling LLP''. July 9, 2025.</ref>

==== Domestic research and experimentation tax deduction ====
The law allows full expensing of domestic research and experimentation expenditures for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2025.<ref name= key/>

The law allows businesses to hold an election to amortize domestic research and experimentation expenditures that are otherwise capitalized (other than property that would be depreciated or depleted) over a five-year period.<ref name= key/>

The law allows certain businesses to elect to claim a tax deduction for unamortized domestic research and experimentation costs in the first tax year beginning after 2024 or ratably over a two-year period.<ref name= key/>

The law allows certain small businesses{{efn|For this purpose, a small business is one with up to $25{{nbsp}}million in average gross receipts during the 3-year period preceding its first tax year that begins after December 31, 2024.<ref name=key/>}} to retroactively expense its domestic research and experimentation costs for tax years that began on or after January 1, 2022.<ref name= key/>

==== Business interest tax deduction ====
The law changes the calculation of the limit on interest expense tax deductions such that deductions for depreciation, amortization, or depletion are excluded when calculating adjusted taxable income.<ref name= key/>

==== Tax deduction for pass-through entities====
The 20% deduction for qualified business income for owners of pass-through entities was made permanent.<ref name= shep/>

==== Tax credit for semiconductor manufacturing ====
The law increases the [[CHIPS and Science Act]]'s tax credit for advanced [[semiconductor]] manufacturing from 25% to 35%.<ref name="Cooper and Dayen 2025"/>

==== Tax deduction for energy efficient commercial buildings ====
The tax credit for energy efficient commercial buildings is no longer available for any property if the construction begins after June 30, 2026.<ref name= FS-2025-05>"[https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/faqs-for-modification-of-sections-25c-25d-25e-30c-30d-45l-45w-and-179d-under-public-law-119-21-139-stat-72-july-4-2025-commonly-known-as-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-obbb FS-2025-05: FAQs for modification of sections 25C, 25D, 25E, 30C, 30D, 45L, 45W, AND 179D under Public Law 119-21, 139 Stat. 72 (July 4, 2025), commonly known as the One, Big, Beautiful Bill (OBBB)]". ''Internal Revenue Service''. August 21, 2025.</ref>

==== Tax credits for affordable housing and poorer neighborhoods ====
The law expands the [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit]] with a housing credit allocation increase and a bond threshold test reduction, projected to add up to 1.22{{nbsp}}million additional affordable rental homes from 2026 to 2035.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wallace |first1=Dirk |last2=Lawrence |first2=Peter |date=26 June 2025 |title=Senate Finance Committee Releases FY 2025 Budget Reconciliation Bill that Includes Permanent LIHTC Expansion, Novogradac Estimates 1.22 Million Additional Affordable Rental Homes over 2026-2035 |url=https://www.novoco.com/notes-from-novogradac/senate-finance-committee-releases-fy-2025-budget-reconciliation-bill-that-includes-permanent-lihtc-expansion-novogradac-estimates-122-million-additional-affordable-rental-homes-over-2026-2035 |website= |publisher=Novogradac |access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref> To incentivize business investments in poorer neighborhoods, the law makes the LIHTC permanent, along with the [[New Markets Tax Credit Program]] and [[Opportunity Zone]]s, restructuring the latter with tighter accountability standards, although the law does not create any new legal incentives for affordable housing or industrial lands cleanup.<ref name="O’Dell 2025">{{cite web | last=O’Dell| first=Kennedy | title=The good, the bad, and the ugly: The 2025 tax bill and smart growth | website=Smart Growth America | date=August 5, 2025 | url=https://www.smartgrowthamerica.org/knowledge-hub/news/the-good-the-bad-and-the-ugly-the-2025-tax-bill-and-smart-growth/| access-date=August 14, 2025}}</ref>

==== Deductions for certain workers' meals ====
The law allows a tax deduction for restaurants and caterers for the cost of providing a free meal to workers while on shift. Companies can also take a tax deduction for the cost of free meals provided to workers on offshore oil rigs and gas platform workers. Companies that are required to provide meals to maritime crew under federal law may also take a tax deduction for the cost of those meals.<ref name= key/>

[[Beauty salon|Beauty service business]]es are now allowed a tax credit for the FICA taxes they pay on their employees' tips that bring them up to the [[U.S. minimum wage|federal minimum wage]]. Prior to this, only [[restaurant|food]] or [[Bar (establishment)|beverage business]]es were eligible for this tax credit. The change is effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.<ref>Yousaf, Muhammad (September 2, 2025). "[https://www.harpercpaplus.com/the-fica-tip-credit-just-got-a-makeover-what-beauty-and-wellness-businesses-need-to-know/ The FICA Tip Credit Just Got a Makeover: What Beauty and Wellness Businesses Need to Know]". ''Harper & Company CPAs LLC''.</ref><ref>"[https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/fica-tip-credit-for-employers FICA Tip Credit for employers]". ''Internal Revenue Service''.</ref>

==== Metallurgical coal tax credit ====
The law establishes a new 2.5% tax credit for [[metallurgical coal]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Megabill's Most Bizarre Fossil Fuel Handout - Heatmap News |url=https://heatmap.news/politics/megabill-metallurgical-coal |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=heatmap.news |language=en}}</ref>{{efn|Metallurgical coal is mostly used for applications such as steel production. ==== Charitable contributions tax deduction ====
As of 2026, corporations may take a tax deduction for charitable contributions for the amount that exceeds 1{{nbsp}}percent of its taxable income and does not exceed 10{{nbsp}}percent of its taxable income. ==== Foreign-derived intangible income ====
The law reduced the tax rate on foreign-derived intangible income to 14{{nbsp}}percent.<ref name= key/>

==== Tax deduction for whaling ====
The law increases the tax deduction for [[whaling]] boat captains increasing maximum deduction from $10,000 of whale hunting expenses up to $50,000.<ref name= faler>{{Cite web |last=Faler |first=Brian |date=June 28, 2025 |title=Alaskan whaling captains score special tax cut in GOP megabill |url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2025/06/28/congress/alaskan-whaling-captains-score-special-tax-cut-in-gop-megabill-00431077 |access-date=June 28, 2025 |website=Politico |language=en}}</ref><ref name= benson>{{Cite web |last=Benson |first=Samuel |date=June 28, 2025 |title=Senate GOP adds SNAP waivers for Alaska, Hawaii in new megabill text |url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2025/06/28/congress/senate-gop-snap-waivers-alaska-hawaii-megabill-00430999 |access-date=June 28, 2025 |website=Politico |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-06-28 |title=Alaskan whaling captains score special tax cut in GOP megabill |url=https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2025/06/28/congress/alaskan-whaling-captains-score-special-tax-cut-in-gop-megabill-00431077 |access-date=2025-12-14 |website=POLITICO |language=en}}</ref>

=== Tax-exempt organizations ===
==== Excess compensation ====
Effective in 2026, certain tax-exempt organizations{{efn|For this purpose, certain tax-exempt organizations are those that are tax-exempt from taxation under any section of [[501(c)]], 521(b)(1), or [[political organization|527]], or that has tax-exempt income described in {{USC|26|115|1}}.<ref name= key/>}} must pay an excise tax on compensation exceeding $1{{nbsp}}million paid to any current and former employee, rather than only to its top five most highly compensated employees for current and prior years.<ref name= key/>

==== Educational institutions ====
The law changes the excise tax on the investment income of tax-exempt educational institutions. There are three different excise tax rates, and the highest excess tax rate is 8{{nbsp}}percent. The excise tax rate depends on the institution's ratio of its investment assets to its eligible students. Institutions with higher ratios are subject to higher excise tax rates.<ref name= key/>

==== College endowments ====
The law increases taxes on investment income from [[college endowment]]s, estimated to raise $761{{nbsp}}million over 10 years. Colleges with more than 3,000 students and an endowment per student ratio of $500,000 would be taxed starting at 1.4%, with the tax rate increasing to 8% for the wealthiest colleges. The original House bill proposed a tax of up to 21% with no exemptions based on size. An exemption for religious colleges was removed for violating the [[Byrd Rule]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 30, 2025 |title=GOP Senators Scale Back Endowment Tax Further |url=https://www.ai-cio.com/news/gop-senators-scale-back-endowment-tax-further/ |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=Chief Investment Officer |language=en}}</ref>

=== Health and welfare ===
==== Medicare drug negotiation ====
The law reverses aspects of Medicare's price negotiation program, allowing more drugs to be purchased without negotiation and increasing costs for consumers. The Congressional Budget Office estimated $5{{nbsp}}billion in lost savings for the government over ten years.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Robbins |first=Rebecca |date=July 3, 2025 |title=Drugmakers Notch a $5 Billion Win in Republicans' Policy Bill |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/03/health/trump-bill-medicare-drug-prices.html |url-access=subscription |access-date=July 4, 2025 |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

==== Medicaid expansions ====
The law establishes a $50{{nbsp}}billion Rural Hospital Fund, up from $25{{nbsp}}billion, to support health care providers in [[rural area]]s, providing a safety net against Medicaid cuts;<ref name=":3" /> and it authorizes CMS to approve new [[Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services waivers|Medicaid HCBS waivers]] to allow non-nursing-home-eligible persons to participate.<ref>{{cite web |first1=Jillian |last1=Kirby Bronner |first2=Courtney |last2=Burke |date=February 26, 2026 |title=Initial Considerations for Adopting the New 1915c Waiver Design as Enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (HR1) |url=https://rockinst.org/blog/initial-considerations-for-adopting-the-new-1915c-waiver-design-as-enacted-in-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act-hr1/ |website= |publisher=[[Rockefeller Institute of Government]] |access-date=February 27, 2026}}</ref>

==== Medicaid restrictions and funding cuts ====
The law cuts over $1.2{{nbsp}}trillion in federal spending,<ref name=":3" /> primarily from the low-income health insurance program [[Medicaid]]<ref name="signed_law"/> and the nutrition funding program [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program|SNAP]].<ref name="snap">{{cite news |last=Lotz |first=Avery |url=https://www.axios.com/2025/07/03/trump-big-beautiful-bill-snap |title=Where SNAP cuts in Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill" could hit Americans hardest |work=[[Axios (website)|Axios]] |date=July 3, 2025 |access-date=July 5, 2025}}</ref> The law:
* Cuts the Medicaid provider tax, which helps states fund their Medicaid costs, from 6% to 3.5% by 2031;<ref name=":3" />
* Adds work requirements for [[Medicaid]] recipients for the first time, with individuals ages 19 to 64 required to work at least 80 hours per month, and this requirement can also be met through volunteer work or school. Some exemptions exist for adults with dependent children ages 14 and under and those with medical conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Konish |first=Lorie |date=June 25, 2025 |title=Congress' 'big beautiful' bill proposes new Medicaid work requirements. Here's what to know |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2025/06/25/congress-big-beautiful-bill-proposes-new-medicaid-work-requirements.html |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=CNBC}}</ref><ref name="Fox, Medicaid work requirements, July 19, 2025">{{Cite news |date=July 19, 2025 |title='Get a job': Medicaid work requirements included in Trump's megabill sparks partisan debate on Capitol Hill |url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/get-job-medicaid-work-requirements-included-trumps-megabill-sparks-partisan-debate-capitol-hill.amp |work=Fox News }}</ref><ref name="USA Today, Millions will lose Medicaid, August 11, 2025">{{Cite news |date=August 11, 2025 |title=Millions will lose Medicaid under Trump's tax law. Here's the final tally |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2025/08/11/millions-will-lose-medicaid-trump-tax-law/85514650007/ |work=USA Today }}</ref>
* Requires states to charge enrollees in Medicaid expansion states with family incomes between 100 and 138{{nbsp}}percent of the federal poverty level up to $35 for each health care service, if they qualify for Medicaid based on income alone.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Galewitz |first1=Phil |last2=Appleby |first2=Julie |last3=Rayasam |first3=Renuka |last4=Wolfson |first4=Bernard J. |url=https://kffhealthnews.org/news/article/one-big-beautiful-bill-medicaid-work-requirements-affordable-care-act-immigrants/ |title=Republican Megabill Will Mean Higher Health Costs for Many Americans |work=[[Kaiser Family Foundation|KFF News]] |date=July 3, 2025 |access-date=July 5, 2025}}</ref>
* Requires states to check eligibility of people on [[Medicaid expansion]] every six months instead of annually;<ref name=":3" />
* Prevents expansion states from using state contributions to pay Medicaid providers higher prices than [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]] would pay;<ref name=":3" />
* Requires minimum staffing ratios for nursing homes;<ref name=":3" />
* Requires a five-year waiting period for [[Green card|green card holders]] before applying to Medicaid, and reduces retroactive Medicaid payments from three months to one month;<ref name=":3" />
* Limits [[premium tax credit]]s for immigrants;<ref name=":3" />
* Reduces Medicaid payments to states with errors and other improper payments;<ref name=":3" /> and
* Prohibits Medicaid from being used for funding [[Planned Parenthood]] and similar organizations for one year.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/5377656-senate-gop-provision-planned-parenthood/|title=Senate bill allowed to 'defund' Planned Parenthood|last=Weixel|first=Nathaniel|date=June 30, 2025|website=The Hill|access-date=July 2, 2025}}</ref> In July 2025, Planned Parenthood sued the Trump administration over the provision and a federal judge issued a temporary [[injunction]] on the provision.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/judge-temporarily-pauses-trump-administrations-planned-parenthood-fund-rcna217512|title=Judge temporarily blocks Trump administration from cutting off Planned Parenthood funding|last=Atkins|first=Chloe|date=July 8, 2025|website=NBC News|access-date=July 8, 2025}}</ref> In September 2025, the [[United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit|First U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals]] overrode the injunction, allowing defunding.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Raymond |first1=Nate |title=Court allows Trump administration to end Planned Parenthood's Medicaid funding|date=11 September 2025 |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/court-allows-trump-administration-end-planned-parenthoods-medicaid-funding-2025-09-11/ |website=Reuters |access-date=25 October 2025}}</ref>

==== Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) ====
The law:<ref name="Mosley 2025" /><ref name="snap" />
* Requires [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program]] (federal food assistance) beneficiaries ages 18 to 64 to work at least 80 hours per month, compared to ages 18 to 54 under current law;<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=June 30, 2025 |title=SNAP Benefits Set to Change in Trump's Tax Bill: What to Know |url=https://www.newsweek.com/snap-benefit-changes-trump-tax-bill-what-know-2092355 |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=Newsweek}}</ref>
* Requires states with an error rate above 6% to contribute to up to 15% of SNAP benefit costs. Alaska and Hawaii received special exemptions for these effective cuts after lobbying from senators [[Lisa Murkowski]] and [[Dan Sullivan (U.S. senator)|Dan Sullivan]];<ref name=":6" /><ref name="faler" /><ref name="benson" />

* Restricts future updates to the [[Thrifty Food Plan]] used to calculate SNAP benefit levels.<ref name=":7" />

==== Health savings accounts ====

In order to qualify, the direct primary care services needs to be for a flat fee of up to $150 per month for a single individual (or $300 per month for multiple individuals). These services are also added to the definition of medical expenses for a [[Health Savings Account|health savings account]].<ref name= venable>Reno, Juliana; Tavares, Lisa A.; Atlas, Harry I.; Aaron, Ryann M. The law creates [[Trump account]]s, a type of tax-advantaged savings investment account.<ref name= taxchanges>{{Cite news|last1=Dore|first1=Kate|last2=Dickler|first2=Jessica|date=July 3, 2025|title=Tax changes under Trump's 'big beautiful' bill — in one chart|work=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/03/trump-big-beautiful-bill-tax-changes.html|url-access=subscription|access-date=July 4, 2025}}</ref>

Any individual is allowed to contribute to a child's account, up to $5,000 per year per child.<ref name= fidelity>"[https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/personal-finance/trump-accounts-big-beautiful-bill New tax law: 4 big changes for families]". ''Fidelity Viewpoints''. [[Fidelity Investments]]. August 1, 2025.</ref><ref name= usnwr>LaPonsie, Maryalene (August 14, 2025). "[https://money.usnews.com/money/retirement/articles/1k-trump-accounts-are-coming $1K Trump Accounts Are Coming: Experts Weigh In on Who Qualifies, Benefits and Drawbacks]". ''[[U.S. News & World Reports]]''.</ref> Employers are allowed to contribute to their employees' accounts and their employees' children's accounts, up to $2,500 per year.<ref name= conner>"[https://www.connerstrong.com/blog/insights-detail/legislative-updates/trumps-administration-new-child-savings-account-program/ Trump's Administration New Child Savings Account Program]". ''Conner Strong & Buckelew''. July 22, 2025.</ref><ref name="adp-early">"[https://www.adp.com/spark/articles/2025/09/early-guidance-issued-under-hr-1-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act.aspx Early Guidance Issued under H.R. 1, The One Big Beautiful Bill Act]". ''[[ADP Inc|ADP]]''. September 2025.</ref> Contributions by an employer count against the $5,000 annual limit per child, but contributions by the federal government do not.<ref name= adp-early/><ref name= jump-start>"[https://www.whitehouse.gov/research/2025/08/trump-accounts-give-the-next-generation-a-jump-start-on-saving/ Trump Accounts Give the Next Generation a Jump Start on Saving]". ''The White House''. August 29, 2025.</ref> As an exception to the annual limit, [[501(c)|tax-exempt organization]]s are allowed to contribute an unlimited amount into a child's account.<ref name= adp-early/>

Contributions into a child's account are allowed until the end of the end of the year in which the child turns 18.<ref name= adp-early/>

The federal government will contribute $1,000 into a Trump account for each U.S. citizen child with a social security number who was born between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2028.<ref name= conner/><ref name= taxchanges/>

Funds in the account must be invested in [[mutual fund]]s or [[exchange-traded fund]]s that mirror the [[S&P 500]] or another U.S. [[index fund|stock index]].<ref name= jump-start/> Investment earnings are [[Tax deferral|tax-deferred]].<ref name= fidelity/>

A child with a qualified disability{{efn|A qualified disability is a disability that qualifies for [[Supplemental Security Income]] or [[Social Security Disability Insurance]] benefits or blindness before the age of 26 is eligible. Qualified disabilities include [[autistic spectrum disorder]], [[asperger's disorder]], [[developmental delays]], [[learning disabilities]], [[intellectual disabilities]], [[schizophrenia]], [[major depressive disorder]], [[Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder]], [[anorexia nervosa]], [[attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder]], [[bipolar disorder]], [[blindness]], [[deafness]], [[cerebral palsy]], [[muscular dystrophy]], [[spina bifida]], [[Huntington's disease|juvenile-onset Huntington's disease]], [[multiple sclerosis]], [[sensorineural hearing loss|severe sensorineural hearing loss]], [[cataracts|congenital cataracts]], [[chromosomal abnormalities]], [[osteogenesis imperfecta]], [[xeroderma pigmentosum]], [[spinal muscular atrophy]], [[Fragile X Syndrome]], [[Edwards Syndrome]], [[cystic fibrosis]], [[Tetralogy of Fallot]], [[hypoplastic left heart syndrome]], [[end-stage liver disease]], juvenile-onset [[rheumatoid arthritis]], [[sickle cell disease]], and [[hemophilia]].<ref>"[https://www.ableunited.com/?faq=what-type-of-disabilities-qualify-for-an-able-account-2 What type of disabilities qualify for an ABLE account?]" ''ABLE United''. February 20, 2019.</ref>}} is allowed to rollover the funds into an [[ABLE account]] when they reach age 17.<ref name= fidelity/>

For other children, rollovers and withdrawals from the account are allowed starting on the January 1 of the year in which the child turns age 18.<ref name= adp-early/> When the child reaches age 18, the funds will be rolled into a [[traditional IRA]].<ref name= fidelity/>

Contributions by the federal government or an employer are tax-exempt (i.e., they are not taxed as income of the child when they are deposited), while contributions by the child or their parents are neither tax-exempt nor tax-deductible (i.e., they are taxed as income of the child or a gift to the child and they come from after-tax funds of the giver).<ref name= usnwr/><ref name= adp-early/>

The law phases out tax credits passed in the [[Biden presidency|Biden]]-era [[Inflation Reduction Act]]. ''U.S. Department of Energy''. 2025.</ref> China's inclusion is notable due to its centrality to many global energy supply chains. [[Electric vehicle]] tax credits would be phased out by September 2025, and [[EV charging]] tax credits would be phased out by June 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |first1=Timothy |last1=Cama |first2=Amelia |last2=Davidson |first3=Nico |last3=Portuondo |date=July 1, 2025 |title=Senate passes megabill after wind, solar changes |url=https://www.eenews.net/articles/senate-passes-megabill-after-wind-solar-changes/ |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=E&E News by POLITICO |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Senate Passes Bill to Scale Back Clean Energy Tax Credits Under Inflation Reduction Act {{!}} Insights {{!}} Holland & Knight |url=https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2025/06/senate-moves-to-scale-back-clean-energy-tax-credits-latest-updates |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=hklaw.com |language=en}}</ref>

[[Green hydrogen]] production credits are terminated by December 2027, rather than 2033. [[Home energy upgrades from public utilities|Home electrification]] credits are terminated by December 2025. Advanced manufacturing, [[carbon sequestration]], [[biofuel]], and [[nuclear power]] credits remain largely intact (nuclear power even gets a new 10% bonus credit), subject to the aforementioned foreign entity of concern rules.<ref name="Pierce 2025-06-04">{{cite web | last=Pierce | first=Heather | title=Here's What it Means for Clean Energy Projects | website=Clean Energy Counsel | date=June 4, 2025 | url=https://www.cleanenergycounsel.com/legal-updates/big-beautiful-bill-heres-what-it-means-for-clean-energy-projects | access-date=August 22, 2025}}</ref><ref name="Thomson Reuters 2025">{{cite web | title=The One Big Beautiful Bill Act: Changing the landscape for US clean energy | website=Thomson Reuters Institute | date=August 11, 2025 | url=https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en-us/posts/sustainability/one-big-beautiful-bill-act-clean-energy/ | access-date=August 22, 2025}}</ref><ref name="Abramowitz Sausen Olaya">{{cite web | last1=Abramowitz | first1=Laurie|first2=David|last2=Sausen|last3=Olaya|first3=Lauren| title=From IRA to OBBBA: A New Era for Clean Energy Tax Credits | website=Arnold & Porter | date=July 22, 2025 | url=https://www.arnoldporter.com/en/perspectives/advisories/2025/07/from-ira-to-obbba-a-new-era-for-clean-energy-tax-credits | access-date=August 22, 2025}}</ref> Fees on [[methane emissions]] that polluters have to pay the government would be postponed for 10 years, while tax credits for biofuels would be extended an additional four years to 2031.<ref name=":3" />

=== Provisions on agriculture ===
The law rescinds unobligated IRA funding for the Conservation Stewardship Program, Environmental Quality Incentives Program, Agricultural Conservation Easements Program, and Regional Conservation Partnership Program, and adds it to the [[USDA]] budget baseline. The OBBBA outlaws climate action-related goals for agriculture. The law also lifts income caps on households that rely on agriculture for more than 75% of their income, potentially empowering [[corporate farming]].<ref name="Mosley 2025">{{cite web | last=Mosley | first=Maggie | title=Trump signs "Megabill" into law, threatening food security and healthcare for millions | website=Sustainable Agriculture & Food Systems Funders | date=July 16, 2025 | url=https://www.agandfoodfunders.org/trump-signs-megabill-into-law-threatening-food-security-and-healthcare-for-millions/ | access-date=August 22, 2025}}</ref>

The law raises reference prices under the Price Loss Coverage and Agricultural Risk Coverage programs, resulting in $54{{nbsp}}billion in additional spending over 10 years.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Clayton |first=Chris |date=July 1, 2025 |title=Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Clears Senate, Sending it Back to House |url=https://www.oklahomafarmreport.com/okfr/2025/07/01/senate-stays-up-late-to-pass-the-big-beautiful-bill/ |website=Oklahoma Farm Report}}</ref> The law increases spending on [[crop insurance]] programs by $6.3{{nbsp}}billion over 10 years and disaster relief programs at [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] by $2.9{{nbsp}}billion in the same timeframe.<ref name=":9" />

=== Leasing and sale of public lands ===
The law requires the leasing of at least 50% of public lands that private companies desire to lease for drilling, mining or logging. It cuts the royalties (the share of revenue) that the [[petroleum industry]] has had to pay for oil and gas extracted from public lands—costing taxpayers around $6 billion over a decade. It cuts the fee per acre that oil and gas companies have had to pay for initiating leasing of public lands. The law reinstates "noncompetitive leasing" of public lands for drilling, mining or logging that allows companies to purchase at a cheap price public lands that were not sold at auction.<ref name="westernpriorities.org">The Center for Western Priorities, 10 July 2025 [https://westernpriorities.org/2025/07/how-congress-and-trump-are-working-together-to-drill-log-and-mine-virtually-all-public-lands/ "How Congress and Trump Are Working Together to Drill, Log, and Mine Virtually All Public Lands" ]</ref>

Over the next decade, the law requires four lease sales to oil and gas companies of lands inside [[Arctic National Wildlife Refuge]], and six lease sales in the [[National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska]] along Alaska's northern coast.<ref name="westernpriorities.org"/>

The law requires the [[Bureau of Land Management]] to hold quarterly onshore oil and gas lease sales.<ref name=":3" />

=== Asylum fees and immigration ===
The law establishes a $100 annual fee to apply for [[Asylum seeker|asylum]], down from $1,000 in the House bill, a $550 fee to apply for employment authorization for asylum seekers and migrants on [[Parole (United States immigration)|humanitarian parole]] or [[temporary protected status]], and a $500 fee to apply for temporary protected status.<ref name=":5" /> It also increases the fees for [[Nonimmigrant visa|non-immigrant visas]] to $250.<ref name=":3" />

=== Student loans ===
The law:

* Pauses a rule issued under the [[Biden administration]] to cancel [[Student loans in the United States|student loans]] if schools engaged in deceptive recruiting;<ref name=":3" />
* Caps unsubsidized student loans for graduate students at $20,500 per year and $100,000 lifetime;<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=What the Senate Republican tax-and-spending bill means for your money |url=https://www.cnbc.com/guide/the-big-beautiful-bill-act-senate-republican/#lower-student-loan-limits-fewer-benefits |website=CNBC |date=July 2025 }}</ref>
* Caps student loans for students seeking [[professional degree]]s, such as [[Medical school in the United States|medical school]] or [[Law school in the United States|law school]], at $50,000 per year and $200,000 lifetime, and eliminates graduate [[PLUS Loan|PLUS loans]];<ref name=":8" />
* Establishes a lifetime student loan borrowing limit of $257,000;<ref name=":8" />
* Restructures income-based repayment programs;<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nova |first=Annie |date=June 20, 2025 |title=Here's what your student loan bill could be under new repayment plan in Republicans' 'big beautiful' bill |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2025/06/20/rap-vs-save-gops-big-beautiful-bill-may-change-student-loan-bills.html |access-date=July 1, 2025 |website=CNBC}}</ref> and
* Expands [[Pell Grant]]s to cover workforce-training programs.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Yahr |first=Natalie |date=July 30, 2025 |title=Workforce Pell grants aim to support shorter-term jobs training and boost lower-income workers |url=https://pbswisconsin.org/news-item/workforce-pell-grants-aim-to-support-shorter-term-jobs-training-and-boost-lower-income-workers/ |work=[[Wisconsin Center for Investigative Journalism|Wisconsin Watch]] |publisher=[[PBS Wisconsin]] |quote=}}</ref>

=== Expansions to 529 education cost plans ===
A [[529 plan]] will be allowed to distribute funds for the cost to attend an elementary or secondary school, including a public, private, or religious school, after July 4, 2025. Eligible costs include tuition, curriculum and curricular materials, books, instructional materials, online educational materials, and tuition for certain tutoring or educational classes outside one's home.<ref name= rudler>"[https://rudler.cpa/understanding-the-new-529-plan-rules-under-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act-obbba-what-rudler-clients-need-to-know/ Understanding the New 529 Plan Rules Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA): What Rudler Clients Need to Know]". ''Rudler PSC''. August 22, 2025.</ref>

A 529 plan will be allowed to distribute funds for eligible costs of a state and federal licensing program, an industry certification program, or a registered apprenticeship program after July 4, 2025. Eligible costs include tuition, fees, books, supplies, required testing, and continuing education needed to maintain the credential.<ref name= rudler/>

===Employee benefits===
====Employer-provided childcare credit====
As of January 1, 2026, the employer-provided childcare credit ({{USC|26|45F}}) is increased from 25% to 40% (or 50% for eligible small businesses{{efn|name=eligiblesmall|An eligible small business has gross receipts of up to $31{{nbsp}}million for the preceding five years. The threshold will be inflation adjusted in future years.<ref name= adp/>}}) of qualified childcare expenses. The maximum employer-provided childcare tax credit is increased from $150,000 to $500,000 per year (or $600,000 for eligible small businesses{{efn|name=eligiblesmall}}).<ref name= adp/>

The act also expands qualified childcare expenses to include contracted third parties that provide childcare to the employees.<ref name= adp/>

====Dependent care flexible spending accounts====
The annual limit for a dependent care [[flexible spending account]] is increased from $5,000 per year (or $2,500 if married filing separately) to $7,500 (or $3,750 if married filing separately).<ref name= shep/>

====Paid leave while on Family and Medical Leave Act leave====
The temporary tax credit for employers who give paid leave to an employee while they are on [[Family and Medical Leave Act]] leave has been made permanent.<ref name= adp/>

In order to qualify for the tax credit, the employer must pay the employee at least 50% of the employee's usual wages. The amount of the tax credit used to be equal to 12.5% of eligible wages paid to an eligible employee, but it now increases by 0.25% for each percentage point paid above the 50% threshold, up to a maximum credit of 25%.<ref name= adp/>

In order to be eligible for the tax credit, the employee must have worked at least six months for the employer, which is up from 12 months previously.<ref name= adp/>

Paid family and medical leave that is required under state or local law is now eligible for the tax credit, as are employer-paid amounts for qualifying paid leave insurance policies.<ref name= adp/>

====Meals====
Food or beverage provided to employees on certain fishing vessels or certain fish processing facilities for the employer's convenience is 100% tax deductible to the employer, up from 50% previously.<ref name=adp/>

====Moving====
Employer-paid moving expense benefits were temporarily considered taxable income to the employee, but they are now permanently taxable income.<ref name= adp/><ref name= shep/> Moving expense benefits for employees who are active-duty members of the [[U.S. Armed Forces]] or members of the [[U.S. Intelligence Community]] continue to be tax-free to the employee.<ref name= adp/><ref name= shep/>

====Bicycle commuting benefits====
For employer-reimbursed bicycle commuting benefits, these payments are considered taxable income to the employee.<ref name= shep/>

====Student loan repayments====
Student loan repayments made by employers to their employees were temporarily tax-free to the employees but they are now permanently tax-free. The tax-free limit per year will be indexed for inflation starting in 2026.<ref name= shep>Aylesworth, Hallie; Bickel, Luke; Chan, Michael (July 24, 2025). "[https://www.laboremploymentlawblog.com/2025/07/articles/employee-benefits/what-employers-should-know-about-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-act-obbba/ What Employers Should Know About the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)]". ''SheppardMillin''.</ref>

=== 1099 reporting ===
A payor must report payments for goods or services via payment apps, online marketplaces, and payments from credit, debit, or gift cards to the [[Internal Revenue Service]] and the payee on [[Form 1099-K]]. The law changes the threshold for reporting; now reporting on Form 1099-K is required if a person received at least 200 transactions and received at least $20,000.<ref name= cole>Cole, Gail (July 30, 2025). "[https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2025/07/30/one-big-beautiful-bill-act-changes-1099-thresholds/165863/ One Big Beautiful Bill Act Changes 1099 Thresholds]". ''CPA Practice Advisor''.</ref>

The law increases the reporting threshold for [[Form 1099-MISC]] and [[Form 1099-NEC]] from $600 to $2,000 in 2026. The threshold will be adjusted for inflation for future years.<ref name= cole/>
